newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firm on upbeat EMU statements.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firm on upbeat EMU statements.

text.p: Irish bonds firmed in line with other European markets on Monday, boosted by weekend rumblings of a softening in Germany's stance on the EMU entry criteria, dealers said.
Dealers said Bunds and gilts were sharply higher, with peripheral markets also gaining from upbeat statements on EMU which improved sentiment towards European bond markets in general.

"Sentiment is more positive on EMU after this weekend's ECOFIN meeting. Italian and Irish bonds are being well bought today. We have seen interest in Irish bonds right across the curve," one dealer said.

By 1500 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 61 pence from Friday's close at 101.63 to yield 6.06 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was up 87 pence from the close at 107.87 to yield 6.82 percent.

Dealers said the fact that a 75 million punt tap by Ireland's National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) in the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 had been completely sold within a 15 minute period earlier on Monday was an indication of the interest in the Irish market.

Under the Maastricht Treaty which set out the economic criteria a country must meet to join EMU from the start in 1999, a key requirement is to bring its fiscal deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product.

After a meeting of European finance meetings in the Netherlands this weekend, German finance minister Theo Waigel was quoted by two British dailies on Monday as saying: "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent. When I said in the past "three percent means three percent", I did not necessarily mean 3.0 percent."
Waigel later termed the newspaper reports "unfair in the highest degree."
Looking ahead, dealers said the market awaited Thursday's Irish March consumer prices data on Thursday and the release of U.S. March retail sales figures on Friday.
